analysis.one_liner: Lets students borrow college loans directly from the federal government, cutting out banks and guarantee agencies.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 20 House cosponsors including one Republican, never got a vote: it sat in the House education committee and then its postsecondary education subcommittee until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the system where students borrow from banks with the federal government guaranteeing repayment, and instead lend federal money directly to students. Subsidized loans would carry a fixed 8% interest rate, borrowers could request graduated or income-based repayment stretched up to 20 years, and all existing loans could be rolled into one consolidation loan. The existing Stafford bank-based loan program would be phased out by mid-1994, and the guarantee agencies that get paid to insure bank loans would see their fees cut.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and their families, especially middle-income borrowers who fall outside traditional need-based aid. They would borrow directly from the federal government at a fixed 8% rate on subsidized loans and a Treasury-based rate on unsubsidized ones, could choose repayment schedules that rise with income or stretch as long as 20 years, and could consolidate loans of $5,000 or more into a single loan with up to 25 years to repay. Colleges would get a flat administrative payment instead of chasing reimbursements.

how_it_helps.text: Subsidized direct loans would carry a fixed 8% annual interest rate, and unsubsidized loans would be priced at the 52-week Treasury bill rate plus 3.25%, set each year by the Education Secretary.

Borrowers could request graduated or income-contingent repayment schedules, with repayment periods extendable to 20 years, and the Secretary would have to notify every borrower entering repayment that these flexible options exist.

Borrowers with at least $5,000 in outstanding student loans could consolidate them into a single loan, with repayment terms of up to 25 years for larger balances and interest rates based on a weighted average of the loans consolidated but never below 8%.

Unsubsidized borrowing would be expanded for graduate students, independent undergraduates, and, in exceptional cases, dependent students whose parents cannot borrow, and parents could borrow unsubsidized loans up to the full cost of attendance.
Institutions at which 30% or more of borrowers default would lose the ability to let their undergraduates take unsubsidized loans, an accountability measure aimed at the worst-performing schools.

analysis.who_pays: The banks, guarantee agencies, and secondary-market institutions that earn fees in the guaranteed Stafford loan system would lose their middleman role: the Stafford program would be terminated by June 30, 1994, and guarantee agencies' administrative allowance would be cut to 0.25% of outstanding loan volume in the meantime. Taxpayers would front the loan capital, since the Education Secretary would fund the program by issuing Treasury-guaranteed obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and guarantee agencies in the loan business

drawbacks.text: The bill phases out the Stafford bank-based program by June 30, 1994, a rapid transition that would leave schools, borrowers, and the Department of Education little time to stand up an entirely new federal origination and servicing operation.

The federal government would become the lender, funded by issuing general obligations of the United States, putting loan capital, servicing contracts, and default risk directly on the government's books rather than spreading it across private lenders and guarantee agencies.

The program's success would depend on the Education Secretary competitively contracting for loan collection, a central data system, and default prevention — functions the private system then performed, with no guarantee the government-run version would collect as well.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers the trade is favorable: a fixed 8% subsidized rate, income-based repayment, and one-loan consolidation are cheaper and simpler than the bank-based system, and cutting out lender and guarantee-agency subsidies removes a large federal cost. The honest objections are about execution, not principle: the government would need to build from scratch the origination, servicing, and collection machinery that private lenders and guarantee agencies had run for decades, and the two-year wind-down was aggressive for a program touching millions of borrowers. A slower phase-in would have reduced that risk without changing the design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 1991, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, and a month later passed to its postsecondary education subcommittee — where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 1993, with no hearings, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert E. Andrews of New Jersey introduced the Middle Income Educational Opportunity Act of 1991 on August 2, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
Twenty representatives cosponsored the bill: 19 Democrats and 1 Republican.
On October 24, 1991, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Postsecondary Education, and no further action was recorded.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without the bill ever leaving committee or receiving a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The guaranteed student loan industry — banks, guarantee agencies, and secondary-market institutions that earn fees originating, insuring, and buying student loans — kept its role intact for the rest of the Congress, and borrowers kept borrowing through the bank-based Stafford system rather than directly from the government.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace guaranteed bank loans with a federal direct loan program, with an 8% subsidized rate and income-contingent repayment.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee / Subcommittee on Postsecondary Education
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its postsecondary education subcommittee on October 24, 1991, and took no recorded action afterward; the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Guaranteed student loan industry (banks, guarantee agencies, and loan secondary market)
against.role: Recipients of fees under the Stafford guaranteed loan system
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against replacing the guaranteed loan system with direct federal lending, which would eliminate their fees and role as intermediaries.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors came from just two parties' ranks — 19 Democrats and a single Republican — and the bill received no floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Guaranteed student loan industry (banks, guarantee agencies, secondary market)
industries.note: The bill terminates the Stafford guaranteed loan program by June 30, 1994 and cuts guarantee agencies' administrative allowance to 0.25% of outstanding volume, eliminating the origination, insurance, and secondary-market fees these institutions earn on federally subsidized student lending. Their loss would have been borrowers' gain, since the middleman subsidies come out of the same federal student aid budget.

Private servicing roles in the guaranteed program would disappear, but the bill requires the Education Secretary to competitively contract with servicing and collection agencies for loan collection, a central data system, and default prevention programs.

Schools would take on loan origination as agents of the federal government in exchange for a flat administrative payment ($20 per borrower per year or a statutory allowance), and could shift Perkins loan repayments into endowments funding Pell, SEOG, and work-study aid. They gain administrative simplicity and a contractual entitlement to payments but bear new origination duties.
